script: Good morning, and welcome to your market briefing for Thursday 24 September. New York was mixed across our watchlist, with the heavier names drifting lower. Nvidia led the falls, down one point four seven percent to about two hundred and twenty six dollars, on volume around zero point seven times average. Apple slipped zero point eight percent to about three hundred and thirty seven dollars, also on lighter than usual turnover. One headline noted Meta putting Apple firmly in its sights with new virtual reality glasses. JPMorgan Chase eased zero point seven three percent to about three hundred and thirty eight dollars, with volume a touch above average. Chief executive Jamie Dimon said artificial intelligence spending could reach one trillion dollars in twenty twenty seven, and warned it could add a little to inflation. On the other side, Microsoft rose zero point five two percent to just over five hundred dollars. Tesla added zero point three two percent to about three hundred and eighty dollars, with a headline flagging a new Supercharger move. Now to London, where energy did the heavy lifting. BP climbed two point eight six percent to about five hundred and fifty eight pence, the standout gain on the watchlist. HSBC added zero point six six percent to roughly fifteen hundred and nineteen pence, with reports it is targeting younger workers through an entry level hiring drive. The falls were led by AstraZeneca, down one point five two percent to about twelve thousand four hundred and eighty pence, alongside news its Trixeo treatment secured approval for asthma in the European Union. Vodafone fell one percent to about one hundred and twenty four pence. Market chatter suggested its OXG earnings were hit by the Drahi stake sale. Unilever was the mildest mover, easing zero point three one percent to roughly four thousand six hundred and eighty four pence, as a McCormick food deal faces a United Kingdom competition review. No volume data was available for the London names today. Closer to home, the ASX two hundred opens at ten o'clock, with local futures pointing to a flat to slightly positive start. At half past eleven we get quarterly Australian job vacancies data from the Bureau of Statistics, watched for signs of a cooling labour market. Miners stay in focus all day, with overnight iron ore and copper moves setting the tone for BHP, Rio Tinto and Fortescue. In New Zealand, the monthly trade balance lands at a quarter to nine, before the NZX opens. This briefing is AI-generated general information only. It is not financial advice.
